content: These outcomes will be derived using concurrent long-regimen controls from the first two quarters of 2017 and historical long-regimen controls from 2016. The estimates will be presented separately, and sensitivity analyses will be conducted only on the concurrent long-regimen controls. Additional sensitivity analyses will examine outcomes at 18, 21, and 24 months post-treatment initiation. This analysis will evaluate key characteristics such as age, sex, HIV co-infection, prior tuberculosis (TB) treatment history, drug resistance patterns, and the province of treatment. This step will help identify systematic differences between groups, including variations in regimen use and provincial treatment outcomes. The findings will guide further adjustments or matching variables, such as adding random effects for the province of treatment or exact matching within provinces. The primary analysis will focus on South Africa and will compare the outcomes of a bedaquiline-containing all-oral short regimen lasting 9–12 months with the WHO-recommended short regimen of the same duration. The approach involves exact matching and propensity score-based matching on covariates such as HIV co-infection, prior TB treatment history, and drug resistance patterns. Additional matching will be performed on age, sex, and baseline sputum smear results. Logistic regression using mixed models will calculate adjusted odds ratios and confidence intervals, while binomial regression will estimate adjusted risk differences. Subgroup analyses will be conducted if sufficient patient numbers are available, focusing on specific drug combinations or individual drugs such as linezolid, delamanid, or carbapenems. If any subgroup analysis includes fewer than 100 patients, it will not be performed. The study will also include sensitivity analyses to relax criteria for country-level income and report outcomes accordingly. Secondary analyses will compare outcomes of a bedaquiline-containing all-oral short regimen lasting 9–12 months with regimens lasting ≥18 months that include bedaquiline and/or delamanid. These analyses will use data from the EndTB observational study, focusing on patients treated from 2013 onward in upper-middle-income countries. Subgroup analyses will examine the use of specific drugs, such as bedaquiline or delamanid, and their combinations. The study acknowledges several limitations. In South Africa, drug resistance testing primarily relies on genotypic methods, which may not detect resistance to drugs commonly used in short regimens, such as pyrazinamide or clofazimine. Adverse events and the acquisition of drug resistance are not reported in the South African cohorts, limiting the analysis of these outcomes. Additionally, comorbidities such as diabetes and mental health disorders are not routinely captured, and extrapulmonary TB is excluded from the analysis. The study will use data from the Nix-TB trial, which assessed a novel 6–9 month regimen of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid in patients with extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) or treatment-intolerant multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB). This trial lacked a comparison group, so outcomes will be compared with matched controls from an individual patient data meta-analysis (IPD-MA) dataset. The IPD-MA includes data from over 13,000 MDR-TB patients and 3,000 pre-XDR and XDR-TB patients treated between 1993 and 2016. The Nix-TB regimen will be compared with four comparator regimens from the IPD-MA, which include various combinations of bedaquiline, linezolid, and other anti-TB drugs. The analysis will account for differences in treatment duration and censor events occurring after the specified analytical duration. Outcomes will be defined according to WHO 2005 criteria, and any discrepancies in outcome classification will be manually verified. The study will assess treatment success, bacteriological cure, adherence, treatment failure or relapse, death, adverse reactions, and the acquisition of drug resistance. However, adverse reactions and drug resistance acquisition cannot be analyzed using the IPD dataset due to data limitations. The Nix-TB trial outcomes will be reclassified according to WHO 2005 definitions and compared with IPD outcomes. Descriptive statistics will examine treatment durations and deviations from intended therapy durations. In summary, this study aims to rigorously compare the efficacy and safety of novel and existing TB treatment regimens using robust statistical methods and comprehensive data sources, while addressing key limitations in the available datasets.
